robodebt-original.answer:
Cabinet approved the scheme, which proceeded without the legislative change the Department of Social Services had said was needed to support income averaging; the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme found it was a costly failure of public administration.

Bill Shorten moved in the House of Representatives on 10 August 2023 that the House accept the royal commission's findings regarding the former ministers involved in the design and implementation of the scheme, and apologise to victims and frontline Centrelink staff.

In its report, the commission concluded that the Ombudsman was deliberately misled, which gave the government further opportunity to resist scrutiny by using his report as a shield.

The Royal Commission's report made 57 recommendations, of which 56 were numbered; the Australian Government's response referred to 56 recommendations, and no government response or implementation document is held.

The Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme was established by Letters Patent on 18 August 2022, with Catherine Holmes AC SC as Royal Commissioner, and reported on 7 July 2023.

Zali Steggall told the House on 11 March 2026 that the National Anti-Corruption Commission's investigation into the robodebt referrals found two public officials engaged in serious corrupt conduct and cleared four others, including former prime minister Scott Morrison.

Mary Doyle told the House on 1 August 2023 that the royal commission led by Commissioner Catherine Holmes had delivered answers for the more than 500,000 victims of the former Liberal government's unlawful robodebt scheme.

robodebt-182.answer:
The commission found the Scheme was approved by Cabinet and proceeded without the legislative change to support income averaging that DSS had said was needed.

The commission concluded robodebt was a costly failure of public administration in human and economic terms.

The Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme (Commissioner Catherine Holmes AC SC) examined who was responsible for the scheme; Kate Thwaites told the House of Representatives on 7 August 2023 that the final report examined 'the establishment of the scheme and who was responsible for it'.

The Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme, whose Royal Commissioner was Catherine Holmes AC SC, investigated who was responsible for robodebt and delivered its final report on 7 July 2023.

Its final report makes 57 recommendations, and 47 hearing transcripts are held as evidence rather than findings.

The commission found the Ombudsman was deliberately misled, letting the Government resist scrutiny by using his report as a shield.

Bill Shorten told the House on 31 July 2023 that the commission went to the role of the member for Cook (Scott Morrison), who as social services minister first took robodebt to cabinet in 2015, and that Commissioner Holmes found he 'allowed Cabinet to be misled' and 'failed to meet his ministerial responsibility to ensure that Cabinet was properly informed'.

Bill Shorten told the House on 10 August 2023 that Commissioner Holmes said the affair showed what 'can go wrong through venality, incompetence and cowardice', and said she reached findings against individuals only with 'a high degree of satisfaction about the evidence' after a fair hearing; Shorten then moved the resolution accepting the findings regarding the former ministers involved in the scheme's design and implementation.

Graham Perrett described the notices to the House on 20 November 2024 as 'these Turnbull-Morrison debt notices', reflecting the scheme's operation under successive Coalition ministers.

Commissioner Holmes stated that the scheme 'made many people feel like criminals', as quoted by Mark Dreyfus in the House on 10 October 2024.
